newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Senate elects Cardoso ally as president.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Senate elects Cardoso ally as president.

text.p: Brazil's Senate on Tuesday elected a close government ally as its president, giving a boost to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's reform programme and a bill allowing his re-election.

Senator Antonio Carlos Magalhaes, who emerged as one of Brazil's most powerful politicians during the 1964-85 military dictatorship and is still known as "The Emperor," won the backing of 52 of the upper house's 81 members. Rival candidate Iris Rezende received 28 votes and there was one abstention.
Magalhaes, addressing the Senate after the vote, pledged support for the government's reform programme.

A bill to modernise the pensions system is awaiting discussion in the Senate while tax and civil service reforms are stuck in the lower house. They are considered vital to Brazil's attempts to reduce public spending and consolidate on two years of low inflation.

"The reforms are ready and waiting ... We will vote on them with the speed the Brazilian people expect of its congressmen," said Magalhaes, now the fourth most senior figure in Brazil's political hierarchy.

He was also expected to clear the way for a constitutional amendment allowing Cardoso to seek re-election in exchange for the declared support for his candidacy of all 13 senators of the president's Brazilian Social Democratic Party.

The amendment was approved by the Chamber of Deputies last week in what was considered the biggest victory of Cardoso's two year's in office. It faces another vote in the lower house before moving on to the Senate.
"Antonio Carlos' administration will be of extreme importance and he will give the government his full support," said the government's leader in the Senate, Elcio Alvarez.

Some observers said the government's relationship with Magalhaes might not always be a calm one. He threatened to reject a $1.2 billion project for an airspace protection system in the Amazon in 1995 until the government bailed out failed bank Banco Economico, based in his home state of Bahia.
Last year he punched a rival senator in the face after a row on the floor of the Senate.

On Wednesday, Magalhaes' son Luiz Eduardo was due to step down as president of the Chamber of Deputies. The government hopes its pro-reform candidate, Michel Temer, will win the race to replace him, leaving allies in charge of both houses.
